title: Latency-aware batching loadgen playground: configs, warmup, and repeatability notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playground doc for experimenting with latency-aware batching in our throughput benchmarking harness. The goal is to capture a minimal, repeatable protocol for runs that stress batching behavior while being sensitive to tail latency noise. This note collects config patterns, warmup recipes, seed hygiene, telemetry alignment, and a short runbook we can iterate on.

Scope and constraints:
- Focus: throughput bench harness runs that intentionally exercise batching decisions (auto-batching, static batch sizes, timeouts).
- Not covered: model-level profiling (operator traces) beyond coarse GPU/host telemetry; separate traces are linked in artifacts.
- Target environments: heterogeneous GPU fleets used by Dedicated and Hosted (A100-40GB, H100-80GB emulated runs).

Why this playground?
We repeatedly see high variance in p95/p99 latency when batching timeouts and sequence length distributions shift. Rather than a single monolithic playbook, this doc tries a family of small, orthogonal experiments to isolate causes: inter-arrival noise, priming state, batch-timeout heuristics, and thermal drift.

High-level hypotheses to test:
1) Short random bursts (poisson arrivals) plus long tails in seq length cause small batches to build slowly and increase p99 by >30% relative to steady arrivals.
2) A short stochastic warmup (randomized priming requests) reduces first-run cache misses and stabilizes p95 but may bias throughput estimates if not anchored.
3) Batching timeouts tuned to 2x mean inter-arrival minimize p95 without large throughput loss for conversational workloads; the optimum shifts with occupancy.

Test environment (baseline):
- Image: bench-2026-02 (runtime + probe harness v3.5)
- Hardware: 1x H100-80GB (dedicated test node), CPU: 64vCPU, NVMe scratch, 512GB RAM
- Runtime flags: --kv-cache-enabled, --auto-batch=true, quantize-path=fp16
- System clocks: chronyd running, nvidia-driver 550.x, CUDA 12.x, nsys v23.2 for traces
- Telemetry: prom/push gateway for request-level metrics, GPU-exporter, perf events, and per-request trace ids inserted by loadgen

Canonical loadgen config patterns (playground variants):
1) latency-sensitive (small batches):
   - arrival: fixed inter-arrival 8ms (125 QPS)
   - concurrency clients: 8
   - request size distribution: short-only (mean tokens 12, stdev 4)
   - target: keep batch-timeout = 5ms, max-batch=32, allow partial-batches=true
   - seed: deterministic seed per run (see RNG hygiene)

2) throughput-max (large batches):
   - arrival: back-to-back (tight loop) with 100 client threads
   - concurrency: high (simulate bursty aggregator)
   - request size: mixed (20% long >256 tokens, 80% short 16 tokens)
   - batch-timeout = 20ms, max-batch=512, allow-batching-by-queue=true

3) hybrid auto-batching probe (latency-aware):
   - arrival: poisson lambda tuned to target QPS
   - dynamic seq-length sampler informed by production fingerprint
   - auto-batch policy = latency-aware (timeout adapt based on recent p90)
   - probe flags: --record-batch-histogram, --report-batch-composition
Minimal config snippet (loadgen-format):
- qps_target: 300
- arrival_dist: poisson
- seq_length_profile: production_sample_v4.json
- rng_seed: 8675309
- warmup: {type: stochastic, duration_seconds: 45}
- telemetry: attach_trace=true

RNG and seed hygiene notes:
- Use an explicit RNG seed for synthetic payload selection and arrival jitter so runs are deterministic when desired. However, to measure variability across natural jitter, we also run a set of randomized-seed runs (N=5) and report mean/SD.
- Seed scoping: keep seeds scoped to the client side only; do not set global seeds that affect kernel-level heuristics (that would reduce realism).
- Anchor runs: before any experimental sweep, run 3 identical seeded anchor runs (seed=same) to ensure harness-level repeatability. If anchor variance >5% p95 across anchors, investigate system-level noise (thermal, co-tenants).

Warmup and priming recipes (three-phase):
1) Primer (short, high-entropy): 30–60s of randomized short sequences at 2x target QPS. Purpose: populate kernel caches, JIT paths, and initial allocator states.
2) Ramp (gradual ramp to target): 2–5 minutes, smoothly increasing QPS to target. Purpose: let runtime stabilize batching heuristics and thermal state.
3) Steady sample window: once metrics indicate plateau (stable p50/p90 for 60s), mark the run start and collect steady-state for configured duration (typically 10–20 minutes for throughput runs, 3–5 minutes for latency-first experiments).

Important warmup caveat: Primer can bias throughput numbers upwards (cache-warm runs benefit). Always report whether primer was used and keep an unprimed control for direct comparison.

Observability signals to capture (minimum):
- request-level: start_ts, end_ts, latency_ms, batch_id, batch_size, seq_length, trace_id
- batch-level: batch_id, kernel_path_taken, batch_timeout_ms, enqueue_wait_ms, nvlink/PCIe stalls
- host: cpu% by process, memory usage, loadavg, disk IO
- gpu: util%, dram_bw, sm_efficiency, power_draw, gpu_temp
- infra: ambient temp, node uptime, recent kernel updates

Analysis primitives and metrics:
- throughput: tokens/sec, requests/sec (token-normalized)
- latency: p50/p90/p95/p99, tail ratio (p99/p90)
- batch metrics: mean batch size, batch size distribution (histogram), fraction of partial batches
- occupancy: fraction of active batch slots filled per step
- stability: rolling CV (coefficient of variation) for p95 across 1-minute windows
- repeatability: anchor-run SD and coefficient of repeatability (CR)

Noise mitigation checklist (pre-run):
- Pin CPU governor to performance; disable turbo for better repeatability when necessary.
- Quiesce non-essential daemons (indexers, backup agents).
- Move test VM to isolated host or isolate NUMA/cpu sets.
- Clear caches that affect the runtime (if testing cold-start behavior, document cache wipes explicitly).
- Ensure Nvidia persistence daemon and power limit are set and stable.

Run protocol (recommended for any experiment):
1) Verify baseline health: run smoke script (5s low-QPS) and check no errors.
2) Run three anchor runs (seed=A) capturing full telemetry. If variance acceptable, proceed.
3) For each config variant: run N=3–5 runs with different seeds (unless determinism is required), collect traces.
4) Post-run: aggregate logs, compute sample windows, produce a single summary CSV row per run for our benchmark dashboard.
5) If a config shows improved throughput but worse tail, run longer duration (x2) to verify effect persists.

Correlating traces and debugging anomalies:
- When p99 jumps: correlate batch composition timeline with nvml/gpu metrics; look for memory copies that coincide with large host-side stalls (enqueue_wait spikes).
- For intermittent high latency: check for rare >1ms spikes in enqueue wait caused by a small race in batch assembly; collect thread-level histograms with perf.
- Use nsys traces limited to a 30s window around an anomaly to avoid huge files. Tag start/end with trace ids matching loadgen timestamps.

Common pitfalls and notes from the field:
- Over-priming: extremely long primers (>5m) can mask realistic cold-cache behavior and produce optimistic throughput numbers.
- Invisible co-tenants: noisy neighbors on shared hosts produce long-tail outliers; prefer dedicated bare-metal nodes for final claims.
- Batch-timeout interactions: lowering the timeout reduces latency but increases CPU interrupts and host overhead; measure host CPU per request.
- Sequence length skew: a few very long requests can dominate batch slots and create head-of-line blocking — sample production distribution carefully.

Quick troubleshooting cheatsheet:
- High baseline p95 across anchors: check node thermal state and recent kernel upgrades.
- Batch size stuck small despite high QPS: inspect client pacing and inter-arrival jitter; ensure per-client clocks are sync'd.
- Throughput regression with same config: verify quantize-path flags, and that the runtime didn't pick a different kernel set (log kernel selection).

Runbook template (one-liner checklist to paste into CI job):
- set_cpu_performance_governor.sh
- stop_nonessential_daemons.sh
- git checkout bench-v3.5 && ./bench/setup-env
- ./bench/run-anchor --config X --seed 42 --duration 180
- iterate configs, collect s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/
- run post-agg script to generate CSV + dashboard upload

Appendix: example analysis commands
- Summarize steady window: python tools/bench_agg.py --input run.json --steady-window 60 --out summary.csv
- Extract batch histograms: jq '.batches[] | {ts, size, timeout}' run.json > batches.ndjson
- Quick plot: tools/plot_latency.py summary.csv --metric p95 --out p95.png

Open questions / next experiments:
- Measure effect of different primer shapes (random short vs. random long vs. production-mix) on both tail and throughput.
- Evaluate an adaptive timeout controller (PID-like) for auto-batching and compare stability against static heuristics.
- Run controlled thermal-experiment: repeat a single config while slowly increasing GPU power limit to see occupancy/throughput sensitivity.

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally a lightweight, iterative playground doc. If we settle on a small subset of configs that show meaningful signal, we should convert the canonical protocol into a templated YAML used by our orchestration (bench-runner) and add strict artifact naming for easier historical comparison.
